question: What is statistical learning, what kinds of problems does it address, and how is the book organised?

limits: Introductory chapter: no experiments, no methods evaluated, no error rates reported; examples are only described.
Prostate data had an error in the first edition (subject 32 lweight), fixed in 2nd edition.
Authors say their exposition reflects a statistics background and that the unsupervised problem is less developed in the literature (as of 2009).
Chapter list predates deep learning; ensemble/random forests called 'recently proposed'.
practices: Understand simple methods before complex ones (p.7, How This Book is Organized).
Read chapters 1-4 in sequence; Chapter 7 (model assessment and selection, bias/variance, overfitting, cross-validation) is mandatory (p.8).
Choose loss asymmetrically where errors differ in cost: in spam filtering, filtering out good email is worse than letting spam through (p.3).
Allow a 'don't know' category so a classifier keeps a very low error rate, with those cases sorted by hand (digits, p.4-5).
For microarray data prefer unsupervised view (cluster samples as points in 6830-dim space) over regression on gene and sample indicators (p.5).
Assume reader has one elementary statistics course including linear regression (p.7).

terms.definition: It is called “supervised” because of the presence of the outcome variable to guide the learning process.
we observe only the features and have no measurements of the outcome. Our task is rather to describe how the data are organized or clustered.
a prediction model, or learner, which will enable us to predict the outcome for new unseen objects. A good learner is one that accurately predicts such an outcome.
supervised problem where the outcome is a class variable such as email/spam
supervised learning problem where the outcome measurement is quantitative
features are predictors (e.g. diet and clinical measurements); training set is data in which we observe outcome and feature measurements for a set of objects
